title: The twenty-minute secret
intro: A short magazine-style article about the afternoon nap and what it can do for your brain. It was written for Psotek English; Ana is a made-up example, not a real person.
paras: Every day at about two o'clock, Ana, an accountant in a busy office, used to hit a wall. Her eyes felt heavy, the numbers on her screen started to swim, and she reached for her third coffee of the day. For years she thought the problem was her lunch or her lack of willpower. Then a colleague gave her some surprising advice: "Stop fighting it. Have a short nap."

The afternoon slump that Ana felt is completely normal. Our body clock does not keep us equally alert all day. Most people have a natural dip in energy in the early afternoon, whether they eat a big lunch or not. In many hot countries, people have long organised their day around this dip, which is one reason why the siesta became a tradition in places such as Spain.

The key to a good nap, however, is its length. Sleep researchers generally recommend between ten and twenty minutes. A nap this short keeps you in light sleep, so you wake up feeling refreshed. If you sleep for much longer, you may fall into deep sleep, and waking up from it can leave you groggy and confused for half an hour or more. Scientists call this feeling "sleep inertia", and it is the reason why some people say that naps make them feel worse.

Timing matters too. A nap in the early afternoon fits the body's natural rhythm, but a nap late in the day can make it harder to fall asleep at night. Some people even try a "coffee nap": they drink a cup of coffee and lie down straight away. Because caffeine takes around twenty minutes to start working, they wake up just as it begins to take effect.

Ana was not convinced at first, but she decided to try it for a month. She set an alarm for eighteen minutes and rested in her car during her lunch break. After a week, she noticed that the two o'clock wall had almost disappeared. She now drinks one coffee a day instead of three. "I used to think napping was lazy," she says. "Now I see it as part of doing my job well."
